```{r setup}
library(EMLMLasso)
```

## Overview

EMLMLasso fits linear mixed models with a lasso penalty on the fixed-effects
coefficients, for clustered or longitudinal data, via an
Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. Random effects are integrated out
at each E-step; the fixed effects are updated at each M-step with a
coordinate-descent lasso fit (`glmnet::glmnet()`) on the random-effects-
adjusted response.

Two functions do the fitting:

* `EMLasso_LMM()` fits the model at a single, user-supplied `lambda`.
* `EMLasso_BIC_Search()` fits the model over a data-driven grid of `lambda`
  values and selects the one that minimizes BIC. This is the recommended
  entry point for most uses, since choosing `lambda` by hand rarely gives
  the best model.

## Simulating example data

`simulate_lasso_lmm()` generates longitudinal data from a sparse linear
mixed model: `p` fixed-effect covariates, only `pstar` of which have a
non-zero true coefficient, plus a random intercept and random slope on
`time`.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(2026)
p <- 10
pstar <- 3
dat <- simulate_lasso_lmm(n = 40, nj = 5, p = p, pstar = pstar, sigmae = 1, seed = 2026)
head(dat)
```

The response is `y`; the grouping variable is `id`; the fixed-effect
covariates are `x1, ..., x10`, of which only `x1, x2, x3` have a non-zero
true coefficient (equal to 1 in this simulation).

## Fitting a single lambda

`formFixed` and `formRandom` are ordinary R formulas. Here `formFixed`
includes all ten covariates, and `formRandom = ~ time` requests a random
intercept and a random slope on `time` (the true data-generating structure).

```{r single-lambda}
fit <- EMLasso_LMM(dat, formFixed = y ~ ., groupVar = "id", formRandom = ~time,
                   lambda = 0.15, verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

`coef()`, `fitted()` and `residuals()` methods are available:

```{r single-lambda-methods}
coef(fit)
```

## Selecting lambda by BIC

In practice, `lambda` is rarely known in advance. `EMLasso_BIC_Search()`
fits the model across a grid of lambda values (sized by `n_lambdas`) and
reports the one with the lowest BIC.

```{r bic-search}
search <- EMLasso_BIC_Search(dat, formFixed = y ~ ., groupVar = "id", formRandom = ~time,
                             n_lambdas = 15)
search
```

The selected model correctly identifies `x1`, `x2` and `x3` as the active
covariates, shrinking the other seven to exactly zero.

```{r bic-search-coef}
coef(search)
```

`plot()` shows BIC across the lambda grid, with the selected value marked:

```{r bic-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot(search)
```

`summary()` gives a more detailed readout of the selected model, including
which covariates were shrunk to zero:

```{r bic-summary}
summary(search)
```

## A note on the random-effects structure

The covariance for cluster/subject $i$ is $\Psi_i = Z_i D Z_i' + \sigma^2 I$, 
with $b_i \sim N(0, D)$ independent of the residual errors. 
`EMLasso_LMM()` and `EMLasso_BIC_Search()` assume Gaussian random effects and errors, and
conditional independence within a cluster given the random effects.

## A real-data example: riboflavin production

`riboflavinV100` (bundled with this package; see `?riboflavinV100`) is a
longitudinal version of the well-known riboflavin production dataset for
*Bacillus subtilis*, with 100 gene-expression covariates as fixed-effect candidates -- a 
high-dimensional (`p >> n`) setting. It is worked through separately in
`vignette("EMLMLasso-riboflavin")`.

## Relationship to Oliveira, Schumacher and Lachos (2026)

This package implements the `EMLMLasso` algorithm introduced in Oliveira
et al. (2026) (full citation below; run `citation("EMLMLasso")` for a
BibTeX-ready entry).

### References

Oliveira DCR, Schumacher FL, Lachos VH (2026). The use of the EM algorithm
for regularization problems in high-dimensional linear mixed-effects
models. *Statistical Methods in Medical Research*, 35(2), 240-254.
[doi:10.1177/09622802251399913](https://doi.org/10.1177/09622802251399913)
